title: Introducing MongoDB Atlas Sharding Advisor: Know When and How to Scale Sharded Clusters
summary:
As applications grow, database teams need to make increasingly complex decisions about how to distribute data, manage workloads, and scale their infrastructure. Sharding enables MongoDB to scale horizontally, but managing a sharded cluster can introduce its own challenges. Understanding cluster health, diagnosing uneven load, and choosing an appropriate shard key can require piecing together metrics across multiple views and relying on specialized expertise.

MongoDB Atlas Sharding Advisor solves this by bringing sharding insights, contextual recommendations, and shard key analysis directly into MongoDB Atlas, helping database teams understand cluster health, identify potential scaling actions, and make more informed decisions as their workloads grow.

Now available for dedicated Atlas deployments running MongoDB 8.0 or later, Sharding Advisor brings together three capabilities: Sharding Insights, Sharding Recommendations, and Shard Key Analyzer.

Figure 1. See how MongoDB Atlas Sharding Advisor helps database teams investigate sharded cluster health, identify potential issues, and evaluate shard key candidates.

Sharding Insights: Clear views of sharded cluster health

Troubleshooting a sharded cluster often means investigating signals across individual shards, collections, and mongos routers. When that information is spread across multiple views, it can be difficult to determine where an issue originates or understand how different parts of the cluster interact.

Sharding Insights brings shard-level, collection-level, and mongos metrics together in a single view in Atlas, giving database teams a clearer picture of cluster health and helping them investigate potential performance and data distribution issues.

With Sharding Insights, teams can:

  • Investigate shard-level performance: Understand whether resource pressure or workload activity is concentrated on particular shards.

  • Understand collection-level distribution: Examine how data and operations are distributed across collections, and identify potential sources of imbalance.

  • Explore mongos behavior: Inspect routing and connection metrics at the entry point to the sharded cluster.

Together, these signals help teams narrow down where to investigate when performance or distribution issues arise, without having to piece together the same information across multiple views. Sharding Insights uses MongoDB Atlas’s existing metrics infrastructure, so there are no additional agents to install or separate telemetry pipeline to configure.

Figure 2. Sharding Insights brings shard, collection, and mongos metrics together in MongoDB Atlas to help teams investigate the health of sharded clusters.

Sharding Recommendations: Identify issues and next steps

Visibility is an important first step, but database teams also need to know which conditions warrant attention and which options to consider. A growing collection, uneven load across shards, or a shard approaching its capacity can introduce operational challenges as workloads evolve. Identifying these conditions and understanding their underlying causes can require manual investigation and specialized expertise.

Sharding Recommendations help teams identify conditions in their clusters that may need attention. For each recommendation, Atlas provides context about why it appeared and suggests potential next steps to help teams investigate and evaluate their options.

For example, recommendations can flag situations like:

  • A collection growing beyond the capacity of a single shard

  • Uneven load across shards

  • Shards approaching capacity

By explaining the conditions behind a recommendation, Sharding Advisor helps database teams move from identifying a potential issue to understanding what they should investigate next. Recommendations provide decision support, not automatic remediation. Teams remain in control of evaluating the suggested actions and determining the right approach for their workloads and operational requirements.

Figure 3. Sharding Recommendations highlights conditions that may need attention, explains why they were flagged, and provides suggested next steps.

Shard Key Analyzer: Make shard key decisions with workload data

Shard key selection is one of the most consequential decisions in designing a sharded collection. A key that doesn’t align well with an application’s data and access patterns can contribute to uneven distribution, hot spots, or inefficient workload routing. Yet evaluating candidate shard keys can be difficult. Database teams need to consider key characteristics and understand how those characteristics relate to their workloads before deciding how to distribute data.

The Shard Key Analyzer brings shard key analysis into MongoDB Atlas, helping teams evaluate candidate keys and understand potential trade-offs before making sharding decisions.

Using MongoDB’s analyzeShardKey command, the analyzer evaluates characteristics such as:

  • Cardinality: How many distinct values a candidate key contains

  • Frequency: How frequently particular key values occur

  • Monotonicity: Whether key values tend to increase or decrease in sequence

When query sampling is configured, the analyzer can also incorporate read and write distribution data to help teams understand how a candidate shard key may distribute workload across shards. It supports single-field, compound, and hashed shard-key analysis, giving teams the flexibility to evaluate different candidates.

By bringing this analysis into Atlas, Shard Key Analyzer helps database teams compare candidates using evidence rather than assumptions alone. The result is a more informed basis for evaluating how a shard key may align with an application’s workload and data distribution needs. Note that Shard Key Analyzer provides analysis to support decision-making; it does not automatically select or apply a shard key.

Figure 4. Shard Key Analyzer evaluates candidate shard keys using key characteristics and, when configured, workload-related read and write distribution data.

Sharding guidance, built into MongoDB Atlas

Sharding Advisor brings visibility, recommendations, and shard key analysis together in the Atlas experience, helping database teams better understand their clusters and evaluate their options as workloads grow.

With Sharding Advisor, teams can:

  • Understand cluster health by bringing shard, collection, and mongos metrics into a unified view.

  • Identify conditions that require attention, along with contextual recommendations and suggested next steps.

  • Evaluate shard key candidates using key characteristics and optional workload-related data.

These capabilities help teams investigate potential issues, assess scaling options, and make more informed decisions about their sharded deployments.

title: Building an Agentic Warehouse Management System—Part 2: Java and Spring AI
summary:
If you arrived here without reading the first part, I recommend starting with Agentic WMS — Part 1: Where AI Agents Add Value. There, we introduced the WMS scenario, explored the replenishment problem, and discussed where an AI agent can add value without replacing deterministic application logic. In this second part, we will move from the design to the first steps of the implementation.

We will look at how the agent is built with Java and Spring AI, how its capabilities and boundaries are defined, how it is triggered by the WMS, and how the planner turns the agent’s goal into an execution plan.

In Part 3, we will continue from that plan and see how the agent executes tasks using controlled tools, gathers the context it needs, makes the replenishment decision, and takes action when necessary.

Designing the agent

From this point on, we will focus on the main parts of the agent implementation using Java and Spring AI. Rather than covering Spring AI from the ground up, we will concentrate on the components directly relevant to this part of our agent: prompts, capabilities, triggering, and planning. For a broader introduction to Spring AI, see this article by my colleague Tim Kelly.

In Part 1, we established an important boundary: the WMS defines what the agent is allowed to do, while the agent decides what to do within those boundaries. Now we can translate that design into code.

Before diving into the implementation, the following diagram summarizes the complete agent flow across Parts 2 and 3. In this part, we will focus on defining the agent, triggering its execution, and creating the plan.

Figure 1. Agent lifecycle: Define, trigger, and plan.

Define the Agent

The agent is triggered after an outbound operation is completed, with the goal of determining whether that operation created a need for replenishment.

The first step is to define how the agent should behave and what it is allowed to do.

In our implementation, we organize the agent around three main components:

  1. Planner

  2. Executor

  3. Reporter

The planner receives the goal and determines the tasks required to achieve it:

The executor will receive one task at a time and perform it using the tools available for that task:

Finally, the reporter summarizes what happened during the execution:

These are simplified versions of the prompts used in the complete application, but they show the responsibility of each component. Together, these components become part of our agent definition:

The definition also contains the capabilities available to the agent. In our replenishment workflow, we use five:

  • Analysis: Access invoices, inventory, and stock movements.

  • Policy: Retrieve depositor policies.

  • Decision: Determine whether replenishment is required.

  • Replenishment: Create a replenishment request.

  • Notification: Draft the related email.

Each capability defines a type of operation and the tools that can be used while performing it:

This gives us a simple boundary around each task. An ANALYSIS task, for example, can access inventory and stock movement tools, but it cannot create a replenishment request. A DECISION task does not expose any tool and uses the results collected by the previous tasks.

Finally, we can connect these pieces when defining the replenishment agent:

At this point, we have defined what the agent can do and the boundaries around those operations. Before looking at how the plan is created, let's see how the agent execution starts.

Trigger the agent

The agent starts after an outbound operation has been successfully completed. Once the transaction is committed, the application publishes the OUTBOUND_INVOICE_COMPLETED event:

A listener receives that event and starts the agent using the outbound invoice number as the reference:

Using AFTER_COMMIT ensures that the agent starts only after the outbound operation has been persisted and the inventory already reflects the latest state. From there, the agent receives its goal and can begin planning how to accomplish it.

Plan

Once the agent is triggered, the first responsibility of the AgentRunner is to create an execution plan.

The application does not define this list of tasks in advance. Instead, the planner receives the goal together with the capabilities available to the agent and determines which tasks are required for its execution.

Each planned task contains two pieces of information: what needs to be done and which capability should be responsible for it:

Based on this information, the planner generates an ordered list of tasks:

Here, Spring AI maps the model response directly to our PlannedTask objects through structured output, giving the application a typed execution plan instead of requiring us to parse generated text manually.

Once the planner returns the tasks, we persist the initial state of the execution as an AgentRun in MongoDB.

At this point, the execution is marked as RUNNING, and every task generated by the planner starts with the PENDING status:

This gives us a persistent representation of the execution from the beginning, including the tasks that were planned. At this point, the document may look like this:

The plan is now ready, and the execution has been registered.

Conclusion

In this second part, we translated the agent design into the first pieces of the implementation. We defined its responsibilities and capabilities, connected it to the WMS workflow, and used the planner to turn the agent goal into a persistent execution plan.

At this point, the agent knows what needs to be done and which capability is responsible for each task. In Part 3, we will focus on how that plan is executed: using controlled tools, gathering operational and business context, making the replenishment decision, and acting when necessary.

title: Agentic Smart Payment Routing with MongoDB / Part I: The Multi-Modal Blueprint
summary:
Transaction routing is a delicate balancing act between authorization rates, execution cost, and latency. A declined transaction can mean a lost sale, making payment optimization one of the most direct levers for top-line revenue growth. Yet payment operations teams remain trapped in manual operational cycles: Pulling batch CSV reports, analyzing spreadsheets, and manually updating rule tables in legacy gateways. And that repetitive cycle can cost you dearly.

Global businesses lose 1.5% to 2.2% of annual revenue to poor payment performance and false declines, according to research by Checkout.com and Oxford Economics.  While those percentages may seem small, it actually adds up to more than $50 billion in lost revenue each year. And the impact isn’t seen in weeks, months, or a year later. In fact, the fallout is immediate: 45% of shoppers abandon purchases and shift to competitors after a single checkout decline.

To recover lost revenue, modern infrastructure must decouple routing intelligence from checkout execution. Running a background multi-agent control plane to analyze telemetry, simulate options, enforce cost guardrails, and update JSON rules in MongoDB enables continuous smart routing optimization with execution in milliseconds.

Welcome to our new series on agentic payment smart routing, where we architect a modern payment routing platform. This first installment introduces the core concepts for designing an AI-driven control plane across all payment modalities. In the following series, we will apply these foundational principles to specialized deep dives into card payment and cross-border bank transfer routing.

Foundational principles of smart routing

To build a resilient payment stack, you need to understand four universal principles that apply whether processing a credit card, a cross-border, or a crypto stablecoin payment. These four principles answer four questions:

  • Where? Routing applies only before the transaction enters the network or rail.

  • Who? Networks, PSPs, and acquirers have distinct roles.

  • What? Input signals map to an output target: a Merchant ID (MID), clearing rail, or blockchain network.

  • When? Before payment entry (prerouting), at initiation (smart routing), and after a recoverable failure (cascading failover)

Figure 1 summarizes these principles:

Figure 1. Foundational principles of smart routing (universal across modalities).

Why do scripted payment routing rules fall short?

Payment routing selects which gateway, acquirer, or network rail processes a transaction from intent to settlement. Choosing the right architecture requires evaluating three distinct paradigms along the maturity spectrum: static, traditional dynamic, and AI agentic routing.

The business objective is to improve authorization rates without allowing processing costs, fraud exposure, or operational complexity to outpace revenue. A declined transaction can mean a lost sale, and poor payment performance erodes revenue through false declines. Yet many payment ops teams still rely on batch reports, spreadsheets, SQL queries, and manually maintained rule tables.

Figure 2. The evolution of payment routing mechanics.

Robotic process automation and scripted workflows face three main limitations in payment routing:

  • Dimensionality explosion: Payment performance can shift at complex intersections, such as a specific clearing rail, jurisdiction, routing identifier (BIN, BIC, or chain ID), asset type, or transaction amount range. A script can only analyze combinations that engineers explicitly anticipated.

  • Unstructured error interpretation: Processing endpoints, banks, and digital asset networks often return inconsistent responses and decline codes. Rigid scripts struggle to process vague signals (such as "Do Not Honor" or generic rejection codes).

  • Multi-constraint trade-offs: Achieving higher authorization rates often comes at the cost of higher processing fees, network wire or gas costs, foreign exchange spreads, volume commitments, or liquidity constraints. Nested conditions quickly become complex to maintain, explain, and test.

Agentic AI bridges this gap, not by replacing fast execution with slow LLM calls, but by handling background reasoning and continuous rule optimization while preserving a fast, predictable execution path.

An agentic control plane and fast data plane help improve payment routing

An agentic architecture separates background payment rule optimization from payment execution. Payment rule optimization is executed at an asynchronous multi-agent control plane, while payment execution runs on a high-speed execution data plane.

The asynchronous multi-agent control plane does not evaluate individual payment requests in real time. Invoking AI agents on the hot execution path would introduce unsustainable processing costs and unacceptable latency for high-volume scenarios. Instead, the control plane operates continuously in the background to monitor route degradation, simulate net-margin impacts, and present optimized routing rules on an operational dashboard for human payment manager approval. Meanwhile, the high-speed execution data plane handles live transactions at the point of interaction—whether at a POS terminal, an e-commerce checkout, a bank transfer portal, or a Web3 payment widget—by deterministically querying active, declarative rules and evaluating relevant context in milliseconds.

Figure 3. High-level architecture of multi-agent control and high-speed execution data planes underpinned by MongoDB and Atlas Agent Engine.

The control plane can automate the five-step payment routing optimization loop typically executed manually by the human payment analyst. The asynchronous multi-agent control plane works continuously in the background. Specialized agents can divide the optimization loop into focused responsibilities:

While this is a simplified example applicable to card payment routing, these concepts can be easily adapted to bank transfers and crypto payments.

A telemetry agent detects that U.K. Mastercard debit transactions have a 78% authorization rate through Gateway Alpha versus a 91% rate through Gateway Beta. The simulation agent estimates moving 50,000 monthly transactions (average $80 value) could recover $520,000 in sales. Gateway Beta charges higher fees, but the 0.18% projected fee increase remains below the 0.5% policy cap. The supervisor agent can present the projection results as a scorecard for approval and then persist an active rule with Gateway Beta as the primary route and Gateway Alpha as the backup.

How MongoDB supports agentic payment routing

Agentic payment routing needs more than a place to store rules. It needs a data platform that unifies telemetry, transaction history, provider profiles, policies, agent state and memory, and active configurations to support investigation and execution.

MongoDB’s document model naturally fits payment data that evolves across providers and rails. An acquirer may return structured decline fields, a clearing house nested ISO 20022 XML error payloads, and a crypto RPC node unformatted event logs. A document model preserves these native payload differences without rigid schema migration or separate extraction pipelines. This flexibility enables AI agents to analyze complete payment context rather than relying only on predefined fields a rigid script anticipated.

MongoDB Atlas brings search and aggregation capabilities together. MongoDB Vector Search helps find similar historical payment contexts, while metadata filters and aggregation pipelines narrow results by country, network, payment modality, currency or token asset, and policy constraints. Agents use these signals to detect hidden performance patterns and rank routes by success rate, similarity, and processing fees.

The database also stores active JSON rules that the execution engine reads. Agents write new rules, record their confidence and justification, set their status to pending approval, and activate them upon manager approval. Time-to-live (TTL) indexes handle rule expiration, while MongoDB Change Streams instantly notify the control-plane components of transaction data or rule updates without waiting for batch jobs.

Deployable anywhere, Atlas Agent Engine is an enterprise platform for managing the full lifecycle of AI agents. It delivers native short- and long-term memory primitives within the database, eliminating custom state pipelines. Running in a sandboxed execution runtime with built-in observability, it enables auditing of agent recommendations. With native safety controls and support for open standards like MCP and A2A, it integrates into existing stacks to deliver secure, audit-ready payment routing.

Security and deployment requirements shape the architecture. MongoDB Queryable Encryption keeps sensitive fields encrypted while supporting specific query patterns, supporting PCI DSS and privacy obligations. Zone-based sharding keeps selected data in target regions, while multi-cloud deployments ensure high availability across cloud providers. These capabilities help build an architecture that meets regulatory, availability, and data residency needs.

Most importantly, MongoDB supports the separation between control and execution. The control plane can analyze telemetry, logs, vectors, and policies, while the data plane retrieves only the active rule and attributes required for a fast decision.

What agentic payment routing enables

Smart payment routing is evolving from static rules into a continuous, self-healing optimization system. Static routing remains useful for deterministic paths, and machine learning can add real-time scoring. But neither approach fully addresses the work of discovering new segments, interpreting changing unstructured decline or failure signals, simulating alternatives, and enforcing competing multi-variable constraints across cards, bank rails, and digital assets.

Agentic AI handles this background work. With a multi-agent control plane and MongoDB, PSPs, orchestration providers, banks, and enterprise merchants can continuously analyze payment performance, test routes, protect margins, and approve impactful changes. MongoDB manages the changing operational context, enables advanced search capabilities across similar payment scenarios, and serves active rules for low-latency execution.

The result is a practical path to smarter payments: Autonomous optimization where reasoning is useful, deterministic execution where speed is essential, and human oversight where governance requires it.

References:

  • Checkout.com: High Performance Payments Report – The Hidden Billion-Dollar Opportunity

  • Checkout.com Newsroom: Research Finds Businesses Lag Behind in Payment Performance

  • Checkout.com Blog: High-Performance Payments: The Hidden Billion-Dollar Opportunity

Figure 3. High-level architecture of multi-agent control and high-speed execution data planes underpinned by MongoDB and Atlas Agent Engine.

The control plane can automate the five-step payment routing optimization loop typically executed manually by the human payment analyst. The asynchronous multi-agent control plane works continuously in the background. Specialized agents can divide the optimization loop into focused responsibilities:

While this is a simplified example applicable to card payment routing, these concepts can be easily adapted to bank transfers and crypto payments.

A telemetry agent detects that U.K. Mastercard debit transactions have a 78% authorization rate through Gateway Alpha versus a 91% rate through Gateway Beta. The simulation agent estimates moving 50,000 monthly transactions (average $80 value) could recover $520,000 in sales. Gateway Beta charges higher fees, but the 0.18% projected fee increase remains below the 0.5% policy cap. The supervisor agent can present the projection results as a scorecard for approval and then persist an active rule with Gateway Beta as the primary route and Gateway Alpha as the backup.

How MongoDB supports agentic payment routing

Agentic payment routing needs more than a place to store rules. It needs a data platform that unifies telemetry, transaction history, provider profiles, policies, agent state and memory, and active configurations to support investigation and execution.

MongoDB’s document model naturally fits payment data that evolves across providers and rails. An acquirer may return structured decline fields, a clearing house nested ISO 20022 XML error payloads, and a crypto RPC node unformatted event logs. A document model preserves these native payload differences without rigid schema migration or separate extraction pipelines. This flexibility enables AI agents to analyze complete payment context rather than relying only on predefined fields a rigid script anticipated.

MongoDB Atlas brings search and aggregation capabilities together. MongoDB Vector Search helps find similar historical payment contexts, while metadata filters and aggregation pipelines narrow results by country, network, payment modality, currency or token asset, and policy constraints. Agents use these signals to detect hidden performance patterns and rank routes by success rate, similarity, and processing fees.

The database also stores active JSON rules that the execution engine reads. Agents write new rules, record their confidence and justification, set their status to pending approval, and activate them upon manager approval. Time-to-live (TTL) indexes handle rule expiration, while MongoDB Change Streams instantly notify the control-plane components of transaction data or rule updates without waiting for batch jobs.

Deployable anywhere, Atlas Agent Engine is an enterprise platform for managing the full lifecycle of AI agents. It delivers native short- and long-term memory primitives within the database, eliminating custom state pipelines. Running in a sandboxed execution runtime with built-in observability, it enables auditing of agent recommendations. With native safety controls and support for open standards like MCP and A2A, it integrates into existing stacks to deliver secure, audit-ready payment routing.

Security and deployment requirements shape the architecture. MongoDB Queryable Encryption keeps sensitive fields encrypted while supporting specific query patterns, supporting PCI DSS and privacy obligations. Zone-based sharding keeps selected data in target regions, while multi-cloud deployments ensure high availability across cloud providers. These capabilities help build an architecture that meets regulatory, availability, and data residency needs.

Most importantly, MongoDB supports the separation between control and execution. The control plane can analyze telemetry, logs, vectors, and policies, while the data plane retrieves only the active rule and attributes required for a fast decision.

What agentic payment routing enables

Smart payment routing is evolving from static rules into a continuous, self-healing optimization system. Static routing remains useful for deterministic paths, and machine learning can add real-time scoring. But neither approach fully addresses the work of discovering new segments, interpreting changing unstructured decline or failure signals, simulating alternatives, and enforcing competing multi-variable constraints across cards, bank rails, and digital assets.

Agentic AI handles this background work. With a multi-agent control plane and MongoDB, PSPs, orchestration providers, banks, and enterprise merchants can continuously analyze payment performance, test routes, protect margins, and approve impactful changes. MongoDB manages the changing operational context, enables advanced search capabilities across similar payment scenarios, and serves active rules for low-latency execution.

The result is a practical path to smarter payments: Autonomous optimization where reasoning is useful, deterministic execution where speed is essential, and human oversight where governance requires it.

title: Scanning 7.25 Million Public Repositories on China's Largest Git Platform for Secrets
summary:
This guest post by independent security researcher Ben Zimmermann was developed in collaboration with the Kingfisher team at MongoDB. Ben specializes in large-scale credential exposure research across public source-hosting platforms.

TL;DR: I scanned 7,256,531 public repositories on Gitee (China's largest indigenous Git hosting platform), using both TruffleHog and Kingfisher, and found 26,400 unique verified-live credentials. Findings included an active organization-admin credential for a major enterprise AI platform and thousands of live cloud provider access keys.

What is Gitee?

Gitee, launched in 2013 by OSChina, was selected by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology as the country's national open-source code hosting platform. Its public API is severely constrained relative to GitHub and GitLab: no paginated projects endpoint, and the on-site code-search feature appears to have been retired years ago. A 2021 attempt to study credential exposure on Gitee concluded that its APIs were too limited to scale the research.

Like any large Git platform, it's an attractive surface for credential exposure:

  • It is Git-based, so secrets buried deep in commit history persist.

  • It hosts millions of public repositories with active commit volume.

  • It has no public equivalent of the platform-vendor secret-scanning partnerships that have become standard on GitHub.

Enumerating millions of Gitee repositories

Gitee's public API is severely limited, so enumerating millions of repositories required combining many surfaces: the only official REST endpoint that returned useful data at scale, the platform's Explore feed, per-user repository and stargazer pages on the website itself, and Gitee's internal Elasticsearch widget that backs the on-site search UI.

Bootstrapping a username corpus

The single official REST endpoint that returned useful data at scale was GET /api/v5/search/users?q=. I hit it with three-character prefix queries (aaa, aab, ..., zzz) and combined the results with usernames extracted from the public Explore feed (/explore/all?order=starred|popular|updated). I then expanded that set via each user's following list and the stargazers of popular repositories. This produced a seed corpus of 1,704,759 usernames.

Scraping per-user pages on the frontend

With the username corpus in hand, two per-user pages yielded repositories: gitee.com/{user}/projects (a user's own repos) and gitee.com/{user}/stared_projects (repos the user has starred). Page 1 of /projects returns full HTML; subsequent pages are AJAX-paginated (X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest). The stargazer-list pages used during username bootstrap paginate the same way, additionally requiring a CSRF token extracted from the page-1 HTML.

Querying the on-site search widget

A large fraction of the platform sits outside the social graph. To reach it, I used the same internal Elasticsearch endpoint that backs Gitee's on-site search UI: so.gitee.com/v1/search/widget/wong1slagnlmzwvsu5ya. It takes a query ID, a q parameter, and pagination via from + size:

Each query returned at most 20 results per page, with a hard cap of 200 results total (from + size <= MAX_RESULTS) regardless of how many matches actually existed. For specific usernames, this was usually fine; for common usernames and trigram prefix queries against the widget, the cap silently truncated results.

Escaping the 200-result cap with bucket splitting

The widget's response includes Elasticsearch aggregations that bucket results by language (编程语言) and license (许可证). For the per-username scrape, when a query was capped, I split it by the language buckets the response already returned:

For trigram prefix queries against the widget (used to surface repos not associated with any user I'd discovered), I extended this into a BFS over a query tree: capped nodes split first by language, then by license, then by deeper prefix until each branch fit within 200 results.

After deduplicating repo IDs across all sources, this produced a working set of 7,256,531 unique public Gitee repositories.

Wiring up the scan pipeline

The next challenge was cloning and scanning the 7.25 million repositories. To do this in a single Python script, I used Modal, a serverless compute platform popular for AI workloads but well-suited to most parallel jobs. I ran TruffleHog and Kingfisher concurrently against every repository for increased coverage. Each surface verified credentials that the other missed, so running both caught more exposed credentials than either alone.

Figure 1. Dual-scanner pipeline architecture.

The Docker image

The container image is a multi-stage build that pulls both scanner binaries from their upstream releases into a single Python base, plus git and OpenSSH for cloning:

The per-repo scan function

A single Modal function bare-clones each repo over SSH and runs both scanners concurrently as subprocesses against the same on-disk clone:

Dispatching 7.25M repos in batches

I split the corpus into 50 batches of ~150K repos and ran them sequentially at a steady 350 concurrent containers. Smaller batches were safer at this scale and easier to resume after interruptions; running larger batches was unstable and would hit clone-side blocks.

Cost and scale

Total wall time: roughly one month of continuous execution. Per-repo clone times were a major contributor: Gitee's servers sit in China, and cross-Pacific network distance plus SSH protocol overhead made each clone materially slower than an equivalent GitHub clone would be. The total cost was $3,097.64, fully absorbed by the $5,000 compute-credit sponsorship from Modal that supported this research. The same Modal + dual-scanner architecture works against most Git hosts with little more than a clone-URL substitution. I used a smaller-scale version of this approach in a prior investigation of Algolia DocSearch admin keys.

The results

Across the 7,256,531 public Gitee repositories scanned, the dual-scanner pipeline surfaced 26,400 unique, verified-live credentials after deduplicating by token value.

Both scanners authenticate each candidate against its vendor's API at scan time (TruffleHog's --only-verified and Kingfisher's --only-valid modes), discarding anything that pattern-matches but fails to authenticate. The 26,400 figure is deduplicated by raw secret value, so duplicates across repositories or scanners count once.

Either scanner alone would have caught only about half of these credentials. The two tools' detector coverage was largely complementary: TruffleHog dominated Alibaba Cloud key detection (9,428 vs. 993), while Kingfisher dominated DeepSeek (2,940 vs. 230), OpenAI (1,198 vs. 150), HuggingFace (154 vs. 1), and Chinese-AI services like Zhipu (1,489 vs. 0) that TruffleHog has no detector for.

Secrets by type

The single most common leaked credential type was Alibaba Cloud AccessKey pairs: roughly 1 in every 766 Gitee repositories contained a verified-live Alibaba Cloud credential.

Figure 2. Credentials by vendor.

A long tail of additional vendors (LangSmith, OpenWeather, Algolia, PostHog, OpenRouter, MySQL, Stripe, Slack, Twitter, and others) accounts for the rest.

Secrets committed by date

The vast majority of verified-live credentials were committed in the last two years. 2025 alone accounts for 12,242 unique credentials, nearly half the entire dataset.

Figure 3. Unique credentials committed by year.

Secrets by committer email domain

Most credentials were committed from personal mail services (qq.com, 163.com, gmail.com), making per-company attribution impossible at scale. The corporate-domain numbers below are a floor; even so, the names span major Chinese and Western tech companies alike.

Figure 5. Unique credentials by committer email domain.

Smaller corporate footprints also appear from Oracle, Apple, Meta, Anthropic, and others, plus Chinese commercial and academic domains.

Comparing Gitee with GitLab and Bitbucket

The closest prior data points come from TruffleSecurity's scan of 5.6 million public GitLab repositories, and a companion Bitbucket scan referenced in that post.

Gitee tops both Western platforms on raw count and per-repository density. One methodology note: the TruffleSecurity scans used TruffleHog alone, while this one used TruffleHog and Kingfisher together. TruffleHog's detector library skews toward Western vendors, and Gitee has heavy Chinese-vendor activity (Alibaba Cloud, DeepSeek, Zhipu, and others) that Kingfisher's coverage helps to surface; stripping our findings to TruffleHog-only puts Gitee at 1.76 per 1,000 repos.

Disclosure

I emailed the vendors with the highest exposure volume in this scan, providing each a coordinated report containing the full list of verified-live credentials associated with their service, along with source-repository metadata to help them attribute affected customers.

Per-developer notification (contacting the committer of each leaked credential individually) was not pursued at this scale. Vendor-side revocation is the more reliable path, since it doesn't require any action from the user who leaked the credential.

At the time of writing, revocation status for the disclosed credentials has not yet been confirmed.

Summary

  • Gitee is a meaningful credential-exposure surface. 26,400 verified-live credentials across 7.25M repositories. Per-repository density higher than comparable published scans of GitLab and Bitbucket.

  • Major tech companies appear in the committer metadata, Chinese and Western alike. The breadth includes Huawei, ByteDance, Google, Microsoft, Oracle, and others, suggesting this is not a purely-Chinese-developer phenomenon.

  • Disclosure paths are asymmetric. Western companies typically have bug bounty programs or accessible security channels. Most Chinese companies don't, leaving leaked credentials without a clear remediation path.

  • The architecture is portable. The same Modal + dual-scanner pipeline works on most Git hosts with little more than a clone-URL substitution; the full scan cost roughly $3,000.

title: DataGrip: a great database IDE to work with MongoDB Atlas
summary:
JetBrains released a new version of DataGrip that includes support for MongoDB and ships with the MongoDB Shell out of the box.

A few months ago, JetBrains released the first version of DataGrip that supports MongoDB. DataGrip is a professional DataBase IDE and is a great tool for advanced data exploration and analytical queries for your data in MongoDB and Atlas.

If you use any of the other JetBrains commercial products for development (e.g. PhpStorm, PyCharm), you can install the Database Tools plugin and work with MongoDB right inside your IDE.

As we announced last week at MongoDB.live, the MongoDB plugin in DataGrip and in the other JetBrains IDE now includes a database console built on top of the MongoDB Shell. This is the result of a close collaboration between engineering teams at MongoDB and JetBrains and we are excited to finally release it to all our users.

With this integration, when you connect to MongoDB and Atlas with DataGrip, you get a console/shell experience that is 100% consistent with what you get in the terminal or in the other MongoDB’s developer tools.

DataGrip and Atlas

When your data is stored in Atlas, navigating through it with DataGrip is extremely easy.

For example, to connect to my free Atlas cluster, I can just grab a connection string from the Atlas UI, use it to add a new data source in DataGrip and I am connected and ready to explore my data.

Using Consoles

If you need to run queries, aggregations, or other database commands, consoles are a great way to do that.

The engineering teams at JetBrains and at MongoDB worked together to bring the new, embeddable MongoDB Shell to DataGrip and use it as the engine behind database consoles. This means the same commands that you can run in the MongoDB Shell are available in DataGrip and the other JetBrains IDEs and you can expect them to work exactly in the same way with the addition of the beautiful UI you are already used to on top.

A great fit for Atlas Data Lake

DataGrip works well MongoDB deployments, whether self-managed or in Atlas. You can also use it with Atlas Data Lake. If you have data is stored in Amazon S3 and you want to query and analyze it with MQL, you can create a Data Lake and start working with it right away.

DataGrip’s search capabilities give you a quick way to find the data you are interested in, and its powerful export tool makes it easy to extract it in the format you need to use it with other tools like Excel, for example.

Get started with MongoDB Atlas and DataGrip

We are really happy with the result of our collaboration with the team at JetBrains and we are looking forward to working more together to bring all the future capabilities of the MongoDB Shell to DataGrip and the other JetBrains IDEs.

You can experience for yourself how DataGrip is a perfect companion for MongoDB Atlas:

  1. Get a free MongoDB Atlas cluster;
  2. Deploy some sample datasets;
  3. Download DataGrip and start working with your data immediately.

title: MongoDB.local London 2024: Better Applications, Faster
summary:
Since we kicked off MongoDB’s series of 2024 events in April, we’ve connected with thousands of customers, partners, and community members in cities around the world—from Mexico City to Mumbai. Yesterday marked the nineteenth stop of the 2024 MongoDB.local tour, and we had a blast welcoming folks across industries to MongoDB.local London, where we discussed the latest technology trends, celebrated customer innovations, and unveiled product updates that make it easier than ever for developers to build next-gen applications.

Over the past year, MongoDB’s more than 50,000 customers have been telling us that their needs are changing. They’re increasingly focused on three areas:

  1. Helping developers build faster and more efficiently

  2. Empowering teams to create AI-powered applications

  3. Moving from legacy systems to modern platforms

Across these areas, there’s a common need for a solid foundation: each requires a resilient, scalable, secure, and highly performant database.

The updates we shared at MongoDB.local London reflect these priorities. MongoDB is committed to ensuring that our products are built to exceed our customers’ most stringent requirements, and that they provide the strongest possible foundation for building a wide range of applications, now and in the future.

Indeed, during yesterday’s event, Sahir Azam, MongoDB’s Chief Product Officer, discussed the foundational role data plays in his keynote address. He also shared the latest advancement from our partner ecosystem, an AI solution powered by MongoDB, Amazon Web Services, and Anthropic that makes it easier for customers to deploy gen AI customer care applications.

MongoDB 8.0: The best version of MongoDB ever

The biggest news at .local London was the general availability of MongoDB 8.0, which provides significant performance improvements, reduced scaling costs, and adds additional scalability, resilience, and data security capabilities to the world’s most popular document database.

Architectural optimizations in MongoDB 8.0 have significantly reduced memory usage and query times, and MongoDB 8.0 has more efficient batch processing capabilities than previous versions. Specifically, MongoDB 8.0 features 36% better read throughput, 56% faster bulk writes, and 20% faster concurrent writes during data replication. In addition, MongoDB 8.0 can handle higher volumes of time series data and can perform complex aggregations more than 200% faster—with lower resource usage and costs. Last (but hardly least!), Queryable Encryption now supports range queries, ensuring data security while enabling powerful analytics.

For more on MongoDB.local London’s product announcements—which are designed to accelerate application development, simplify AI innovation, and speed developer upskilling—please read on!

Accelerating application development

Improved scaling and elasticity on MongoDB Atlas capabilities

New enhancements to MongoDB Atlas’s control plane allow customers to scale clusters faster, respond to resource demands in real-time, and optimize performance—all while reducing operational costs.

First, our new granular resource provisioning and scaling features—including independent shard scaling and extended storage and IOPS on Azure—allow customers to optimize resources precisely where needed. Second, Atlas customers will experience faster cluster scaling with up to 50% quicker scaling times by scaling clusters in parallel by node type.

title: Getting Started With MongoDB and AWS CodeWhisperer
summary:
Amazon CodeWhisperer is trained on billions of lines of code and can generate code suggestions — ranging from snippets to full functions — in real-time, based on your comments and existing code. AI code assistants have revolutionized developers’ coding experience, but what sets Amazon CodeWhisperer apart is that MongoDB has collaborated with the AWS Data Science team, enhancing its capabilities!

At MongoDB, we are always looking to enhance the developer experience, and we've fine-tuned the AWS CodeWhisperer Foundational Models to deliver top-notch code suggestions — trained on, and tailored for, MongoDB. This gives developers of all levels the best possible experience when using AWS CodeWhisperer for MongoDB functions.

This tutorial will help you get AWS CodeWhisperer up and running in VS Code, but CodeWhisperer also works with a number of other IDEs including AWS Cloud9, AWS Lambda console, JupyterLab, and Amazon SageMaker Studio. On the Amazon CodeWhisperer site, you can find tutorials that demonstrate how to set up AWS CodeWhisperer on different IDEs, as well as other documentation.

Note: Amazon CodeWhisperer allows users to start without an AWS account because, usually, creating an AWS account requires a credit card. Currently, CodeWhisperer is free for individual users. So it’s super easy to get up and running.

Installing Amazon CodeWhisperer for VS Code

CodeWhisperer doesn’t have its own VS Code extension. It is part of a larger extension for AWS services called AWS Toolkit. AWS Toolkit is available in the VS Code extensions store.

Step 1. Open VS Code and navigate to the extensions store (bottom icon on the left panel).

Step 2. Search for AWS CodeWhisperer, and it will show up as part of the AWS Toolkit.

Step 3. Once found, hit Install. Next, you’ll see the full AWS Toolkit Listing.

Step 4. Once installed, you’ll need to authorize Amazon CodeWhisperer via a Builder ID to connect to your AWS developer account (or set up a new account if you don’t already have one).

Using AWS CodeWhisperer

Navigating code suggestions

With Amazon CodeWhisperer installed and running, as you enter your prompt or code, CodeWhisperer will offer inline code suggestions. If you want to keep the suggestion, use TAB to accept it. AWS CodeWhisperer may provide multiple suggestions to choose from depending on your use case. To navigate between suggestions, use the left and right arrow keys to view them, and TAB to accept.

If you don’t like the suggestions you see, keep typing (or hit ESC). The suggestions will disappear, and Amazon CodeWhisperer will generate new ones at a later point based on the additional context.

Requesting suggestions manually

You can request suggestions at any time. Use Option-C on Mac or ALT-C on Windows. After you receive suggestions, use TAB to accept and the arrow keys to navigate.

Getting the best recommendations

For best results, follow these practices.

  • Give Amazon CodeWhisperer something to work with. The more code your file contains, the more context CodeWhisperer has for generating recommendations.
  • Write descriptive comments in natural language — for example.

Or

  • Specify the libraries you prefer at the start of your file by using import statements.

  • Use descriptive names for variables and functions.
  • Break down complex tasks into simpler tasks.

Provide feedback

As with all generative AI tools, they are forever learning and forever expanding their foundational knowledge base, and MongoDB is looking for feedback. If you are using Amazon CodeWhisperer in your MongoDB development, we’d love to hear from you.

We’ve created a special “codewhisperer” tag on our Developer Forums, and if you tag any post with this, it will be visible to our Amazon CodeWhisperer project team, and we will get right on it to help and provide feedback. If you want to see what others are doing with CodeWhisperer on our forums, the tag search link will jump you straight into all the action.

We can’t wait to see your thoughts and impressions of MongoDB and Amazon CodeWhisperer together.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter: Durable Session Storage for Agents
summary:
The Claude Agent SDK is a package that lets you embed Claude Code's own agent loop directly into your application: web search, file search, file editing, MCP server connections, and more, all without having to define those tools or manage the agent loop yourself. The SDK also automatically persists session transcripts to the local file system by default. Claude calls it the Agent SessionStore.

Today, we are excited to announce the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter, available in Python (with TypeScript coming in January 2027).

What is the Claude Agent SessionStore?

But first, let's understand what a SessionStore actually is. It is the extension point in the Claude Agent SDK for saving an agent's session outside the machine where it ran. Configure one, and the SDK mirrors every conversation turn and action as the agent works, so the session can pick back up exactly where it left off, on any instance that has access to that store.

That matters most once an agent stops running on a single, persistent machine. Say a team deploys their Claude agent as a Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation is a disposable instance; there's no local disk to store anything between calls. Without a SessionStore, each request is stateless by default; the agent has no memory of what came before. With a configured SessionStore, any invocation can pick up a session's full history, regardless of which instance handled the last turn.

That is the gap the MongoDB Session Adapter closes.

This is especially useful for enterprises that have multiple teams developing agents across many machines, who need session storage that survives host failures, scales as the agent fleet increases, and enforces the same access controls and retention rules as the rest of their data estate, not a bolt-on system built solely for agent memory.

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter gives Claude agents durable session storage: a record of the conversation and its action history that lets an agent pick back up exactly where it left off, whether that's on the same laptop, a different server, or any server in a distributed deployment.

The adapter helps cover three crucial areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: Whether a different backend instance picks up a conversation after a restart or a user resumes on a different device, session state doesn't live on the machine that started it. Because every step is mirrored to MongoDB as it happens, any instance in your deployment can resume exactly where the last one left off.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container gets rescheduled mid-conversation, nothing is lost. Entries are written to MongoDB as they occur, not batched or cached locally, so whichever instance picks the session back up sees the same state as the failed one, up to the last completed step.

  • Retention and auditability: Many teams need to retain agent transcripts to meet internal data-retention or audit requirements. Instead of standing up a separate system just for that, session data lives in the MongoDB cluster you're already operating, under the same access controls and backup policies as the rest of your data.

How it works

title: How MongoDB Fits into the EU Sovereign Cloud Ecosystem
summary:
The question of what the term “sovereign cloud” means in Europe has moved from policy debates to formal European Commission (EC) procurement frameworks and industrial investments. The Cloud Sovereignty Framework (CSF), Sovereignty Effectiveness Assurance Levels (SEAL), and the developing EU Cybersecurity Certification Scheme for Cloud Services (EUCS) are separate initiatives that provide distinct reference points. Alongside strategic capital mobilization under the Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP), they establish a clearer direction for critical cloud infrastructure. While specific to EU institutional tenders and funding programs rather than acting as universal mandates, this combined momentum offers IT leaders and enterprise architects across regulated sectors a concrete reference point for how sovereignty criteria shape long-term architectural thinking. These developments help illustrate that operating in a regulated market does not mean every workload must remain on-premises; instead, they demonstrate that sovereignty is a spectrum, helping organizations evaluate the specific level of data control their architecture truly requires.

As organizations evaluate these models, the critical question is not just which infrastructure provider can meet tech sovereignty expectations, but whether the rest of the technology stack upholds that sovereignty posture once workloads are deployed. This is where the database layer becomes a critical consideration, and where MongoDB provides key capabilities to define who has operational custody of data and how seamlessly workloads adapt to evolving governance requirements.

In April 2026, the European Commission awarded sovereign-cloud contracts under the Cloud III Dynamic Purchasing System and used SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 as practical reference points in its CSF for that procurement. This provides a concrete example of how sovereignty-related criteria can be evaluated in an EC-level procurement context. It also raises a practical architectural question: if sovereign-cloud requirements are being evaluated against the CSF as a benchmark, what does that mean for the rest of the technology stack, and especially for the database tier?

This overview examines the potential implications of the awarded landscape, the operational relevance of SEAL-2 and SEAL-3*, and how MongoDB deployment models can support different architectural approaches for organizations to evaluate against their own requirements.

Why the new procurement benchmark matters

The Commission selected several European provider groups for this initiative. These included:

  1. Post Telecom (headquartered in Luxembourg), working alongside OVHcloud and CleverCloud (both based in France).

  2. STACKIT, the cloud division of Schwarz Group, based in Germany.

  3. Scaleway, the cloud arm of Iliad Group, based in France.

  4. Proximus, based in Belgium, partnered with S3NS (a joint venture of Thales and Google Cloud in France), Clarence (Luxembourg), and Mistral (France).

As published in the European Commission’s report under reference IP/26/833, three of the four awarded groups achieved the reported assessment level of SEAL-3, while the Proximus consortium attained SEAL-2. The Proximus result of SEAL-2 is an assessed level within the CSF, not a failed outcome; the consortium’s remaining non-EU dependencies distinguished it from the groups assessed at SEAL-3. Together, these results show that the procurement considered a range of sovereignty postures rather than a simple pass-or-fail threshold, and may help inform future market expectations around sovereignty-driven infrastructure and digital resilience.

In environments governed by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), and the Network and Information Systems Directive 2 (NIS2), where requirements vary by organization and industry, engineering teams face concrete design priorities: mitigating ICT third-party concentration risk, establishing tested exit strategies, or enforcing granular boundaries over data access and telemetry. The CSF evaluation offers technical leaders a reference point for examining these operational dependencies, informing technical due diligence across database tiers and multi-cloud strategies without prescribing a single deployment model or replacing organization-specific legal analysis.

The challenge: infrastructure certification does not cover the full stack

Using cloud infrastructure assessed in the European Commission’s procurement event addresses only part of the broader sovereignty discussion and does not automatically answer questions about every layer of the technology stack. The relevant considerations can include data residency, service operation, metadata flows, external control-plane dependencies, encryption, access controls, and workload portability if requirements or risk posture change.

The database tier is particularly important in a broader data-sovereignty assessment because it stores, processes, and governs access to the data itself. An infrastructure-focused assessment such as the CSF evaluation can provide useful information about the underlying cloud environment, but it does not by itself characterize the database service’s data paths, plaintext exposure, key management, backups, logs and metadata, support and control-plane dependencies, or workload portability.

Regulatory frameworks such as the US CLOUD Act (Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act, enacted in 2018) have heightened enterprise sovereignty concerns over access to data held by providers subject to foreign jurisdiction under applicable legal processes, illustrating why physical data residency alone does not establish operational or jurisdictional control. One practical question is therefore not whether a platform carries a universal “sovereignty” label, but which controls and operating boundaries an organization must evaluate for its own environment. Variables such as control-plane dependencies, cross-region support access, cloud provider corporate jurisdiction, and cryptographic key custody must be individually assessed based on the organization's unique requirements. An organization may adopt cloud infrastructure aligned with SEAL-3 expectations and still find that database-layer telemetry, external support paths, or unencrypted metadata introduce unintended exposures. The infrastructure assessment and the database governance posture remain separate engineering challenges that require independent validation.

MongoDB's three roles in the European sovereign cloud ecosystem

MongoDB serves three distinct roles in the European sovereign cloud ecosystem when viewed through the lens of the European Commission’s CSF. MongoDB’s flexible document model and query API can remain consistent across deployment models, while the operating model, responsibilities, data flows, access controls, and contractual arrangements may differ.

Figure 1. MongoDB deployment modes.

Role one: DBaaS on SEAL-3 sovereign clouds

In this model, a European cloud provider—such as STACKIT, OVHcloud, or Scaleway—operates a MongoDB database service under its own brand, infrastructure, and legal entity. MongoDB supplies the database engine, compatibility guarantees, and technical support framework, while responsibility for operating the service remains with the European provider.

Because the European provider operates the service, it is the entity with operational custody of customer data in this model. MongoDB is a software supplier and does not have operational custody of customer data on the European-operated service. All three provider groups that achieved SEAL 3 for the purposes of the April 2026 EC procurement event include a MongoDB Certified DBaaS partner. For organizations seeking sovereign cloud environments aligned with SEAL-3-style expectations, MongoDB is already available through those partnerships, without workarounds, unsupported deployments, or vendor substitution.

However, architecture teams must carefully evaluate the specific database edition offered by each sovereign cloud provider. Managed offerings in the European ecosystem typically fall into two categories: DBaaS based on MongoDB Community Server and DBaaS powered by MongoDB Enterprise Server, which is the engine underlying Enterprise Advanced. While both editions share the same flexible document model and core query API, they differ significantly in built-in operational capabilities. Community Server provides core database functionality, but achieving enterprise-grade security and operational maturity requires teams to build and manage custom configurations for auditing, access controls, and maintenance. In contrast, DBaaS powered by Enterprise Server delivers turnkey features, including native enterprise auditing, advanced authentication integration, and enhanced operational tooling, representing the closest functional equivalent to MongoDB Atlas in a self-contained or sovereign environment.

Currently, European providers like STACKIT and OVHcloud, alongside providers like IONOS, offer DBaaS backed by Enterprise Server, whereas Scaleway provides managed Community Server with enterprise-grade offerings currently in development. Role two: MongoDB Atlas with sovereignty controls

MongoDB Atlas is a multi-cloud intelligent data platform with availability across Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP). Atlas provides data placement controls; Resource Policies can restrict cluster creation to approved EU regions, and zone-based sharding can support regional data placement, subject to the workload’s shard key and application design.

For encryption, MongoDB Atlas supports Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) integration with cloud provider key management services, which can keep encryption keys outside MongoDB’s direct control. Atlas also supports Client-Side Field Level Encryption (CSFLE) and Queryable Encryption (QE), which encrypt sensitive fields on the client side before data reaches the database. MongoDB cannot access plaintext for those protected fields during supported query operations.

BYOK, CSFLE, and Queryable Encryption (QE) can materially reduce data-layer disclosure risks by preventing unauthorized or platform-level access to plaintext data. However, the effective protection boundary depends on the key-management model, query capabilities, and whether sensitive metadata remains exposed.

Certified DBaaS and Enterprise Advanced are alternative deployment models to evaluate for workloads where data sovereignty and encryption considerations are material. The appropriate choice depends on the organization’s technical, contractual, operational, and legal requirements.

Role three: MongoDB Enterprise Advanced for maximum jurisdictional control

MongoDB Enterprise Advanced (EA) is a commercial subscription that grants organizations the right to run MongoDB on their own infrastructure: on-premises, in a private cloud, on a sovereign provider’s dedicated environment, or in an air-gapped facility. MongoDB does not operate the customer’s clusters and, in this model, does not have operational custody of customer data at rest.

The infrastructure operator remains responsible for the environment in which the clusters run. How access to customer data and any legal or regulatory request would be handled depends on the applicable law, contractual arrangements, and the specific operating model; the relevant custody and control analysis therefore focuses on the entity operating that infrastructure rather than treating MongoDB as the infrastructure operator.

Enterprise Advanced preserves the same document model and core query semantics as MongoDB Atlas, supporting strong application-level portability across deployment models. Organizations can typically move regulated workloads from Atlas to EA while preserving the application data layer and most core query logic, which can reduce redesign effort and support portability, exit planning, and concentration-risk evaluation. The relevance of these capabilities to any particular regulatory framework depends on the organization’s specific requirements and legal and operational analysis.

Aligning the deployment model to your sovereignty requirements

The three MongoDB deployment models offer different combinations of deployment location, operational control, data access, encryption, and portability, which organizations can evaluate against their own data or technology sovereignty-related requirements.

For organizations evaluating technical, contractual, operational, or procurement requirements associated with SEAL-3-style sovereign infrastructure, the Certified Database as a Service (DBaaS) path provides MongoDB capability through a European provider, previously assessed at SEAL-3 in the Commission’s April 2026 procurement.

For organizations evaluating a US-operated managed cloud service with technical controls, MongoDB Atlas with Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), Client-Side Field Level Encryption (CSFLE), and Queryable Encryption (QE) can provide data-layer protections relevant to that assessment.

For organizations evaluating greater direct jurisdictional control, air-gapped operation, or self-managed deployment on sovereign or private cloud infrastructure, Enterprise Advanced preserves the same core document model and query semantics as Atlas and supports application portability without requiring MongoDB to operate the customer’s clusters. Depending on the deployment environment, it can also support customer-managed infrastructure and avoid dependency on a public cloud service, with no MongoDB operational custody of customer data at rest.

A practical advantage is that these three models are not mutually exclusive. An enterprise may evaluate a mixed deployment approach, such as using Atlas for standard workloads in EU-approved regions, Certified DBaaS for higher-sensitivity workloads, and Enterprise Advanced for classified or air-gapped workloads, while application-layer portability and governance requirements may vary by tier.

Final thoughts

Europe’s sovereign cloud ecosystem now includes an example of a formal assessment used in the European Commission’s procurement, four Commission-selected reference providers, and other national frameworks applicable in specific member states. These developments may be relevant to how regulated organizations evaluate cloud infrastructure over the coming years.

MongoDB is present at the database tier through Certified DBaaS partnerships with providers that have been assessed at SEAL-3 in the Commission’s April 2026 procurement, available with technical controls on managed cloud through MongoDB Atlas, and deployable in customer-managed environments through Enterprise Advanced. Each deployment model presents different technical, contractual, and operational characteristics for organizations to evaluate against their own requirements. Each preserves the same core document model and query semantics, which may help reduce redesign effort when moving workloads across deployment models.

*Within the CSF, the SEAL levels range from SEAL-0 to SEAL-4 and describe varying degrees of EU jurisdiction and control over legal, operational, and supply-chain dependencies. At SEAL-2 (Data Sovereignty), EU law is enforceable, though some material non-EU dependencies persist. SEAL-3 (Digital Resilience), assesses whether relevant non-EU dependencies have been reduced to marginal levels under the CSF. SEAL-4 (Full Digital Sovereignty), represents the theoretical goal of complete EU control without critical dependencies on non-EU entities, a standard no provider has reached so far. These descriptions refer to the CSF framework and the assessment made in the Commission’s procurement context; they do not prescribe what any particular organization must do.

  4. Proximus, based in Belgium, partnered with S3NS (a joint venture of Thales and Google Cloud in France), Clarence (Luxembourg), and Mistral (France).

The CSF evaluation offers technical leaders a reference point for examining these operational dependencies, informing technical due diligence across database tiers and multi-cloud strategies without prescribing a single deployment model or replacing organization-specific legal analysis.
